## Two families of test

The tests for cross-sectional dependence split by whether the units are
**ordered** [@pesaran2015, p. 784]. The CD test, the LM tests and the
exponent α treat the units as an unordered set: they ask whether the
units move together, and how pervasively, without a notion of who is near
whom. On a map they detect *whether anything exists*, never whether it
has spatial structure.

That is not a small gap. The implicit null of the CD test is *weak*
dependence, α below 1/4 when N and T grow together [@pesaran2015,
p. 786], and spatial processes generate weak dependence [@pesaran2015,
sec. 30.3.3]. From the other side, @pesaran2015 [p. 839] find the CD test
to be the panel unit-root diagnostic *most robust to* spatial
alternatives, which is to say it does not fire on them. A spatial panel
can pass the CD test and still be spatially dependent in every residual.
The ordered family exists for that case.

## 1. The ordered statistics

Put the map in. @pesaran2015 [eqs. 30.40–30.41] give two forms. The first
is Moran's *I* on the panel,

$$
CD_{\text{Moran}} = \frac{\sum_t \sum_{i \ne j} w_{ij}\, \hat u_{it}\hat u_{jt}}
  {\sqrt{\,\cdot\,}},
$$

the covariance of each residual with its neighbours' average, scaled to a
standard normal [@kelejian1998]. For large N it is equivalent to the
Lagrange multiplier test of @burridge1980, which is the `lme` statistic of
the [lag-or-error section](index.qmd#sec-sp-lag-or-error). The second is
the **local CD** statistic: the CD average restricted to pairs that W
links, with the weights kept,

$$
CD_{P,\text{local}} = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\sum_{i<j} w_{ij}}}\
  \sum_{i<j} w_{ij}\,\hat\rho_{ij}.
$$

What **plm** implements as `pcdtest(w = )` is the binary version:
`w` is passed through `as.logical()`, so every non-zero cell becomes 1
and the statistic averages the correlations of the linked pairs with
equal weight [@croissant2019, sec. 10.1.2.1]. It tests the neighbourhood
*structure*. The weighted form of eq. 30.41 and $CD_{\text{Moran}}$ are
not implemented in this book's tools.

## 2. Why local CD over-reads a factor

Local CD inherits the CD test's virtue, exact centring for any T, and
adds one of its own: it has power on cross-sectionally demeaned data,
where global CD is dead by construction [@croissant2019, sec. 10.1.2.2].
It also has a specific blind spot. If a factor moves every unit, every
pair of units is correlated, neighbours included. Local CD then averages
"a subset of spatially related pairs from a population of correlated
ones", and rejects, favouring a spatial reading of what is not spatial
[@croissant2019, sec. 10.1.2.2]. On the raw house-price index it gives
z = 37, with the national force still in the data; on the CCEMG residuals
it gives z = 28, with the force out. Only the second number is evidence
about geography, and nothing in the first number says so.

## 3. The randomised-W test

@millo2017 turns the blind spot into a test. Under the null that the map
does not matter, the units are **exchangeable**: hand each state a random
set of "neighbours" by permuting the order of the units, and the local
statistic should look the same. Compute it under B shuffled maps, $\tau_1,
\dots, \tau_B$, and compare with the value under the true map, τ. The
one-sided pseudo-p-value, for the usual alternative of positive spatial
dependence, is [@croissant2019, eq. 10.1]

$$
p^{+} = \frac{1 + \sum_{h=1}^{B} \mathbf{1}[\tau_h \ge \tau]}{B + 1};
$$

the two-sided version takes absolute values of cross-sectionally
demeaned data, and the asymmetric version counts each tail separately
[@croissant2019, eqs. 10.2–10.3]. `rwtest` defaults to `alternative =
"twosided"` and to `test = "rho"`, the average correlation of the linked
pairs; `"cd"` and `"sclm"` use the local CD and scaled-LM statistics
instead.

The test is robust to what local CD is not. A factor moves the whole
distribution of shuffled statistics, true map included, so it cancels in
the comparison; serial correlation does the same. That is why @croissant2019
[sec. 10.1.2.2] run it on the MG residuals, with the factor still in
them, and get the same p = 0.002 as on the raw index. It is the test that
displaces local CD as the primary tool, and local CD becomes the
statistic that the shuffle is applied to.

Its limits are the ones its construction implies. With B = 999 the
smallest p-value is 0.001 and the pile has 999 points; with the default
B = 99 it is coarse. It reads W through `as.logical()` like `pcdtest`, so
it never tests a weighting scheme. And it tests one order of
neighbourhood at a time; `order = 2` shuffles the second-order map.

## 4. Before and after the fit

The same two tests serve twice [@croissant2019, sec. 10.1.2]. On the raw
data, or on residuals from which a factor has been removed, they say
whether a spatial model is called for. On the residuals of the spatial
model, they say whether it did its job. The second use has a trap. A
spatial error model's residuals $u = y - X\hat\beta$ are spatially
correlated *by construction*: the model says $u = (I - \lambda
W)^{-1}\varepsilon$, so a residual test on $u$ rejects whenever the model
is right. What the model claims to be free of spatial correlation is
$\varepsilon = (I - \hat\lambda W)u$, period by period, and that is what
the check must test. On the transformed house-price panel the local CD of
$u$ is 32 and that of $\varepsilon$ is 0.5; on rice, 47 and −0.5. A
spatial lag model's residuals $y - \hat\rho Wy - X\hat\beta$ are already
the innovations, and need no filter.

## If / then

| If | Then |
|---|---|
| CD does not reject and the units sit on a map | Nothing is settled; run local CD and the shuffle [@pesaran2015, p. 839] |
| Local CD rejects on raw data with α near 1 | A factor is in the way; defactor first, or read the shuffle, never local CD alone |
| The shuffle rejects on MG residuals | The dependence follows the map, factor or no factor |
| The shuffle does not reject | Space adds nothing; the dependence is a factor, or noise; robust standard errors |
| Checking a spatial error fit | Test the filtered innovations $(I - \hat\lambda W)u$, not $u$ |
| Checking a spatial lag fit | Test the residuals as they are |
| Negative spatial dependence is plausible | `alternative = "symmetric"` or the asymmetric form; the one-sided test can miss it |
| W carries distances | Both tests drop them; report that only the structure was tested |

## Open

- **The weighted local CD and $CD_{\text{Moran}}$** of @pesaran2015
  [eqs. 30.40–30.41] are not implemented; a hand-coded version would have
  no target beyond agreement with the binary one.
- **Robinson's quadratic forms** [@pesaran2015, p. 815] are not
  implemented.
- **Higher orders.** The shuffle at `order = 2` tests the
  neighbours-of-neighbours map, which is the natural follow-up when the
  first-order test rejects and the question is how far the dependence
  reaches. No published number exists for it on either panel.

## Next

A rejection says the dependence follows the map. Which equation it belongs
in is the next note: [spatial model choice](theory-spatial-model-choice.qmd).
